To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the incidence of genetic disease in humans is difficult to determine, but it can be estimated crudely by using data from large-scale studies and more reliably by using data from smaller studies that focus on certain disorders, and that population monitoring for environmental mutagens should focus on sentinel phenotypes such as retinoblastomas and nephroblastomas.

the incidence of genetic disorders in human populations is not precisely known and that the incidence of sporadic cases arising from fresh mutation can be used to monitor the human environment for mutagens.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following aspects of the epidemiology of genetic diseases: (a) the total frequency of all genetic diseases; (b) the total frequency and the individual frequency of specific genetic disorders with early-onset; and (c) the frequency of sporadic genetic diseases with early onset.

the following: (1) the frequency of genetic diseases in the population, (2) the effect of environmental mutagens on the incidence of genetic disorders, and (3) the use of sentinel phenotypes for the monitoring of the human population for the possible effect of environmental mutagenesis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no adequate data for the total frequency of all genetic diseases in human population.
there is no satisfactory information on the incidence and prevalence of genetic diseases in the general population, although some data are available on certain monogenic disorders.

the total number of genetic disorders in a population is difficult to determine, and that it would be useful to have a better knowledge of the frequency of those genetic diseases with early onset and that are easily detected and diagnosed.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the current state of our knowledge of genetic diseases is insufficient to assess the possible magnitude of the genetic hazards caused by man-made mutagens.

, in the absence of a reliable and valid estimate of the total incidence of genetic diseases in a human population, it is not possible to assess the possible contribution of environmental mutagens to the total frequency.
the current state of knowledge is inadequate for the assessment of genetic hazards from environmental mutagens.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, in the absence of a reliable estimate of the frequency of genetic disease in the population, it is impossible to assess the possible impact of environmental mutagens on the incidence of these diseases.

the frequency of genetic diseases in the human population has to be determined by a large-scale population study, and that the data should be analyzed in terms of the age-specific incidence of the disease.
, in addition to environmental mutagenesis, the incidence of genetic disease in human populations may change as a result of other factors.
